title: Toxic Shame
description: What you feel is not ordinary guilt for having done something wrong. It is a bone-deep sense that you yourself are wrong, bad, and undeserving of love.
mechanism: When an emotional flashback is triggered, toxic shame often becomes the strongest and most central feeling. It frequently originates from early experiences of contempt, neglect, or verbal injury.
healingDirection: Quiet the inner critic and practice self-compassion. Interrupt self-attack with healthy boundaries, and respond to the wounded part with your adult self.
safePractice: When the self-attacking voice appears, gently label it: "This is the inner critic." Place a hand on your chest and say: "I am willing to begin treating myself differently."

title: Fear in Emotional Flashback
description: A single sentence or glance suddenly pulls you back into that small, frightened feeling. Your body reacts before your mind does—you want to flee or shrink.
mechanism: When old fear is triggered by the present situation, the nervous system rapidly enters high arousal, producing intense unease or even panic.
healingDirection: First recognize "this may be an old wound being triggered," then use grounding to bring the body back to the present and build a sense that "I am safe now."
safePractice: Press both feet firmly into the ground. Slowly exhale while counting to four. Repeat several times, then quietly say: "I am safe now. This is a memory."

title: Despair in Emotional Flashback
description: It feels like falling into a deep well—nothing you do will matter, nothing will get better. Your body wants to hide or becomes heavy and numb.
mechanism: When despair becomes the main triggered feeling, people often enter a state of deep powerlessness and the urge to withdraw.
healingDirection: Recognize that this is old helplessness being activated, not the whole of present reality. Use the smallest possible action to restore a little sense of "I can still choose."
safePractice: Write down "I am still here," then do one tiny completable thing (drink water, open a window, stand and take two steps).

title: Helplessness & Powerlessness
description: You feel you can do nothing, as if pinned in place. You know what should be done yet cannot move.
mechanism: During intense emotional activation, people often re-experience the smallness and powerlessness of childhood. Trauma also weakens the sense that "I can influence outcomes."
healingDirection: Rebuild agency through tiny choices that are fully under your control.
safePractice: Move a finger or a toe. Feel "I can still control this small part of my body," then do one small thing decided entirely by you.

title: Small, Young & Vulnerable
description: Suddenly you feel very small and young, like a child who needs protection yet has no one to protect them.
mechanism: When old wounds are triggered, body and mind easily regress to the state of early threat.
healingDirection: Respond to that young part with your adult self, letting it know "I am here now."
safePractice: Gently place a hand on your heart or arm and say to the young part inside: "I see you. I am here."

title: Abandonment Depression
description: When things grow quiet, emptiness and pain rise up—like reaching the dead end of a blind alley, helpless and hopeless.
mechanism: This deep emptiness and pain often relate to early emotional neglect or abandonment, and surface more easily when alone.
healingDirection: Keep company with the emptiness instead of rushing to fill or escape it. Allow the process of mourning to unfold slowly.
safePractice: Place a hand on your chest and say: "I am willing to stay with this emptiness rather than immediately flee or fill it." Allow yourself a few quiet moments.

title: Complex Abandonment
description: Shame, fear and melancholy tangle together, making you both want closeness and want to run. The inside feels chaotic.
mechanism: When multiple old emotions are triggered at once, people often fall into the contradiction of longing for connection while fearing injury.
healingDirection: Name the feelings first, then look at them separately instead of being overwhelmed by the whole mass.
safePractice: On paper write "shame," "fear," and "melancholy" separately, then tell yourself: "They can exist at the same time. For now I am only looking."

title: Self-Hatred / Self-Loathing
description: It is not merely dislike of yourself. It is a visceral aversion and the urge to attack yourself.
mechanism: When the inner critic becomes extreme, people develop intense aversion and aggression toward themselves.
healingDirection: Identify and label the inner critic, and redirect the aggression away from yourself.
safePractice: When self-attack appears, clearly say: "This is the inner critic." Then place a hand on your chest and remind yourself: "I deserve to be treated more gently."

title: Self-Abandonment
description: You always put others first. You may not even notice when you are hungry, tired or in pain—essentially abandoning yourself.
mechanism: If you were long neglected early on, it is easy to learn to satisfy others first and lose awareness of your own needs.
healingDirection: Re-learn to bring "yourself" back into view, starting with small bodily signals.
safePractice: Ask yourself three questions: "Am I hungry? Tired? Do I need rest?" Then respond to at least one of them.

title: Inner Critic Attack
description: That voice in your head that constantly finds fault and says you are not good enough is often the internalization of early criticism.
mechanism: The inner critic usually comes from the attitudes of important early figures. It tries to "protect" you by attacking you, at the cost of ongoing self-depletion.
healingDirection: Notice its appearance with mindfulness, then interrupt it with gentle firmness.
safePractice: When it appears, first name it "This is the inner critic," then interrupt with a short sentence: "I do not need to treat myself this way."

title: Social Anxiety
description: In front of others you constantly feel scrutinized, fear saying the wrong thing, fear being seen through as "not good enough."
mechanism: When shame is strong, attention in social settings easily focuses excessively on "how others see me."
healingDirection: Lower the catastrophic expectation of being "found out," while building new experience through small doses of authentic exposure.
safePractice: Prepare one simple opening line or exit phrase in advance to reduce the fear of the unknown.

title: Shame-Based Anger
description: Anger that rises quickly when you feel exposed, criticized or small—often a secondary reaction to underlying shame.
mechanism: When toxic shame is activated, anger can surge as a way to regain a sense of power or to push the threat away.
healingDirection: Look beneath the anger for the shame or fear it is protecting, and respond to that deeper layer.
safePractice: When anger flares, pause and ask: "What just made me feel small or exposed?" Name that softer feeling first.

title: Anger & Aggression
description: A surge of heat, the urge to push back, control, or strike—whether expressed outward or turned inward.
mechanism: Anger is a boundary-protecting emotion. In trauma it may become either chronically suppressed or easily explosive.
healingDirection: Allow anger to exist as information about boundaries, and find safe ways to express or channel it.
safePractice: In a private, safe space (journal, shower, alone), allow yourself to speak the angry words without having to justify them.

title: Freeze Response
description: You know you should act, flee or speak, yet the body feels pinned and unable to move. Energy is stuck.
mechanism: Freeze is a survival response. Uncompleted fight-or-flight energy can remain held in the body.
healingDirection: Respect the freeze. Do not force movement. Gently mobilize only when the body shows readiness.
safePractice: Allow yourself to stay still at first and simply breathe. When the body feels even a little ready, make the smallest possible movement.

title: Overwhelm / Collapse
description: You feel you are about to fall apart. Emotion, pressure and fatigue surge together; you want to cry or drop.
mechanism: When the nervous system exceeds its window of tolerance, collapse or overwhelm can appear as a protective shutdown.
healingDirection: Reduce input, restore basic safety and regulation, then return to one small manageable piece.
safePractice: Stop adding new tasks. Sit or lie down. Name three things you can see right now. Breathe out longer than you breathe in.

title: Numbing & Dissociation
description: You are not "over it"—you feel switched off. Joy and sadness both become muted, as if behind a layer of cotton.
mechanism: To survive unbearable pain, the nervous system may turn down the volume on feeling.
healingDirection: Gently reconnect with bodily sensation without forcing yourself to "feel more."
safePractice: Notice one small physical sensation (temperature of the hands, the rise and fall of the breath). Simply notice, without judging or demanding change.

title: Fawning / People-Pleasing
description: You keep others happy, give constantly, and lose track of yourself—"If I am good enough, you will not leave."
mechanism: When love and safety once depended on pleasing others, fawning can become an automatic survival strategy.
healingDirection: Practice keeping a little space for yourself in small matters, and experience that relationships do not instantly collapse when you are imperfect.
safePractice: Today, respond to one small request with "I need to think about it first," then notice what happens in your body.

title: Flight Response
description: The strong urge to escape—leave the room, leave the conversation, leave the feeling—before anything is resolved.
mechanism: Flight is a survival response. When old danger is sensed, the system prioritizes getting away.
healingDirection: Acknowledge the urge to flee, then experiment with staying for one more breath or one more minute when it is actually safe.
safePractice: When the urge to leave arises, pause and name it: "This is the flight response." Then decide whether leaving is necessary or whether you can stay a little longer.

title: Fight Response
description: The body braces to confront, argue, control or overpower. Softness feels dangerous.
mechanism: Fight is a protective mobilization. In trauma it can become a default way of creating safety through dominance or control.
healingDirection: Redirect the protective energy from controlling others toward protecting your own real boundaries.
safePractice: When the fighting energy rises, ask: "What am I actually trying to protect right now—my boundary or my sense of control?"

title: Hypervigilance
description: You are always scanning for danger, reading faces, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Rest feels unsafe.
mechanism: After prolonged threat, the nervous system can remain on high alert even when the present is relatively safe.
healingDirection: Gradually teach the body that periods of safety can exist, using repeated experiences of "nothing bad happened."
safePractice: Once a day, deliberately look around and name five things that indicate you are safe in this moment.

title: Body Memory Trigger
description: A smell, posture, tone of voice or sensation suddenly floods the body with old feeling before the mind understands why.
mechanism: Trauma is stored not only in narrative memory but in the body. Sensory cues can reactivate those implicit memories.
healingDirection: Orient to the present with the senses, and remind the body that the danger is not happening now.
safePractice: Use 5-4-3-2-1: name 5 things you see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste.

title: Emptiness & Hollowness
description: There is a hollow place inside that nothing seems to fill. Everything feels muted, as if living on mute.
mechanism: Emptiness often relates to emotional numbing, early neglect, or long-term suppression of feeling.
healingDirection: Keep company with the emptiness rather than rushing to fill it with activity, consumption or relationships.
safePractice: Do not hurry to fill it. Simply sit with the emptiness for one minute and notice whether anything shifts.

title: Helplessness
description: The sense that "nothing I do will matter." The feeling of being able to choose or act has gone missing.
mechanism: Repeated experiences of powerlessness can erode the belief that one can influence outcomes.
healingDirection: Rebuild the sense of "I can affect things" through tiny choices that are fully under your control.
safePractice: Do one small thing you can completely control (what to wear, what to drink, which task to do first).

title: Powerlessness
description: You feel stripped of influence. Decisions, outcomes and even your own reactions seem outside your hands.
mechanism: Chronic powerlessness in early environments can leave a lasting imprint on the sense of agency.
healingDirection: Reclaim micro-agency: start with the smallest domain where choice is still available.
safePractice: Choose one tiny preference today and honor it without explaining or justifying it to anyone.

title: Self-Doubt
description: You constantly feel you have not done well enough, chosen wrongly, or are not smart enough. Decisions loop endlessly.
mechanism: When self-worth is fragile, the mind keeps second-guessing to avoid the pain of being "wrong."
healingDirection: Practice making "good enough" decisions and tolerating the residual uncertainty.
safePractice: Set a short time limit for a small decision, choose, and then deliberately stop reviewing it for the rest of the day.

title: Perfectionism Pressure
description: You push yourself with relentless standards. Rest feels like failure; "good enough" feels dangerous.
mechanism: Perfectionism often serves as a strategy to avoid shame or criticism by staying ahead of judgment.
healingDirection: Experiment with deliberate imperfection in low-stakes areas and observe that the feared catastrophe does not occur.
safePractice: Intentionally leave one small task "good enough" rather than perfect, and notice what the inner critic says.

title: Emotional Numbing
description: Feelings are distant. You know you "should" feel something, yet the volume is turned very low.
mechanism: Numbing is a protective adaptation when feeling was once too costly or unsafe.
healingDirection: Invite sensation back in small, tolerable doses without demanding full emotional intensity.
safePractice: Once a day, ask: "What am I sensing in my body right now?" Stay with the answer for three breaths.

title: Fear
description: A tight, source-less tension that makes you want to flee or shrink. The body reacts before the mind understands.
mechanism: Fear is a life-protecting signal, yet when old wounds are triggered it may be out of proportion to present reality.
healingDirection: Build a sense of "secure base" so the body knows there is somewhere safe to return to.
safePractice: Identify one safe object or place and tell yourself: "I can return here." Actually feel its presence.

title: Suppressed Anger
description: The fire held at the bottom—afraid to express, quick to self-blame the moment it rises.
mechanism: When anger is chronically suppressed it may turn against the self or erupt unpredictably. Healthy anger is a guardian of boundaries.
healingDirection: Allow anger to exist and express it in safe ways instead of continuing to suppress or convert it into self-blame.
safePractice: In a safe private setting, allow yourself to speak the angry words without needing to make them reasonable.

title: Grief / Sadness
description: A heavy ache in the chest. You want to cry but cannot, or once you start you cannot stop.
mechanism: Grief is a natural channel for releasing loss and pain. Suppressing it keeps the pain stuck in other forms.
healingDirection: Allow tears and sadness to move rather than suppressing them or rushing to "cheer up."
safePractice: If tears will not come, simply allow the feeling of "wanting to cry" to be present—neither forcing nor immediately stopping it.

title: Guilt
description: You quickly assume it is your fault, rush to apologize, and when someone is unhappy your first thought is "Did I cause this?"
mechanism: If you were early on made responsible for others' emotions, it is easy to take on excessive responsibility.
healingDirection: Distinguish what truly belongs to you from what has been over-assumed.
safePractice: Ask: "If someone else were in the same situation, would I blame them the same way?" Use that standard to reassess.

title: Everyday Shame
description: A lighter, everyday sense of not being good enough, of being about to be found wanting—less bone-deep than toxic shame, yet still draining.
mechanism: Everyday shame is a common background tone when self-worth is fragile.
healingDirection: Practice being seen in your imperfection and accumulate new corrective experiences.
safePractice: Share one small imperfection with a trusted person and practice being seen without being abandoned.

title: Despair
description: The deep-well feeling that "nothing I do will help; it will never get better."
mechanism: When hope has been repeatedly defeated or old helplessness is triggered, despair can become the dominant feeling.
healingDirection: Shrink the time scale to "today" and counter global hopelessness with the smallest possible action.
safePractice: Do only the smallest step available today. Do not look at the future. Do not demand that you feel hopeful.

title: Feeling Wronged / Unseen Hurt
description: You are hurting yet cannot speak it. You hold it in, convinced that speaking would change nothing.
mechanism: When important feelings went long unanswered, it is easy to learn to swallow the sense of being wronged.
healingDirection: First give your own feelings the recognition they need, then decide whether to share them with others.
safePractice: In a journal write: "Today I felt wronged because..." Write it only for yourself—complete one act of self-recognition.

title: Unworthiness
description: When something good arrives, the first reaction is "I don't deserve this" or "They will eventually see I am not that good."
mechanism: When self-worth is built on "I must be good enough to be accepted," it becomes hard to receive what rightfully belongs to you.
healingDirection: Practice receiving kindness without explanation or refusal, challenging the automatic "I don't deserve it."
safePractice: Accept one small kindness or compliment. Say only "thank you"—no explaining, no refusing, no diminishing yourself.

title: Fragile Self-Worth
description: Self-worth feels like thin ice. The slightest breeze cracks it. It needs constant external approval to stay intact.
mechanism: When self-worth depends mainly on outside evaluation, it becomes unstable and easily shattered.
healingDirection: Through steady small self-affirmations, gradually thicken the inner sense of worth.
safePractice: Each day write down three things you did, however small, as an internal record.
